flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me a little about yourself and why early childhood education matters to you.
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q1 Attempt 1]
I've been drawn to early childhood education since I was a child myself. I went through some difficult times as a high schooler, and the way I grounded myself was by volunteering in my previous elementary school. And from there, I started doing Special Olympics coaching, and I coached U5 soccer, and I really wanted to pursue it later on. I had to take a small step away from it when I had children of my own, and I had to get a hysterectomy. And so it was just a really hard balance. But now that my children are older, I have one in junior high and one in high school, I'm finally able to return back to child development and early childhood education. So I'm really excited to be back in there and working with kids again.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Why are you applying to our company, Launch Pad Learning?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q2 Attempt 1]
It's all part of life. We just kind of have to keep rolling and find the good. I've been looking through a lot of schools. I do try to stay away from, there's a majority of the schools in Southern California nowadays are Montessori programs and I'm really big on playing through exploration and being able to interact with one another and so while I completely understand the Montessori method, it's just not quite as play based as I would like and so I really enjoy being able to do circle time with the kids and nurture their individual needs because you know every child is so different it's really hard to put them in a very rigid structure like that and so I just want to be able to get more on their level and when I was looking for schools this school was one of those.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
So when I was working at Magic Carousel, one of the boys that we had in an older grade was struggling a lot. He was in the process of being diagnosed with autism. It was really hard because he didn't have extra assistance with him. And he would get very frustrated because he couldn't quite understand how to tie his shoes yet. So we ended up having him just come and sit with me sometimes in my class to kind of give him a little more, he needed an extra person. He needed to feel a little extra secure. And so my husband and I ended up taking cardboard and drawing out a shoe and putting holes. And so he would practice tying his shoes with me for at least 20 minutes every day out of the school day. So that way he wouldn't feel as behind and have as many meltdowns. Because it was a really big trigger for him when they would kind of be on him about it. So I just tried to sit with him, make sure he had patience and understanding. Make sure I was always getting down on my knees when I was talking to him because anyone standing over him made him very anxious. And so it was just kind of a nice way to make him feel like he had a person inside of the building that was safe for him.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time you felt overwhelmed or stressed at work with children present. What did you do to manage, not the kids, but yourself and your stress?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q4 Attempt 1]
So I spent 10 years volunteering and working with children through SC1 all the way through SC7 in the special education department. There was a couple occasions where children were just very physical, very touchy-feely. And so you get a little touched out after a while, especially when they're older children. And I'm talking around like 10 to 15. So there were a lot of times where we would just create like a tag-out system. So that way, if we started to get a little touched out and a little overstimulated ourselves as adults, we would just kind of like tag each other out to give each other space so we could take a moment and hang out with a child that was a little less contact. Other than that, I think for me, it's mainly just always remembering that children are the ones who are the most important part of our lives. And I think that's really important. Children are just learning the world around them and trying to remember what may not seem as big of a deal or as stressful to us as adults. This is their first time encountering it. And so it's just kind of grounds me that way and reminds me that if it feels big to me, it feels bigger to them. I normally just kind of, I enjoy singing songs with the kids. flow_transcript_slices.question: Imagine you’re caring for a child who clearly does not want to be touched during a routine task, like diapering, helping with clothing, or guiding them physically. They are pulling away or crying. Walk me through exactly what you would do and say, step by step
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q5 Attempt 1]
I think it's really important, especially when doing intimate acts, like changing them, because for a child, if you're a stranger, it's very difficult. I would start by establishing trust with the child, making sure they understand that what we're going to do, I talk them exactly through it so that way nothing feels like it's happening to them, but they're a part of the process. If it's an even younger child that seems to be going through stress and not handling the situation well, it really varies upon the child and the age. Infants, you would sing them songs, soothe them, try to find little things that will kind of relax them in the moment. For older children, like two to three, it's definitely including them in the process so they feel like they have autonomy over the situation.

[Q6 Attempt 1]
I did get constructive feedback when I was, there was a child that was colicky. And as a mom, my instinct was just to hold and pat the whole time. And I got the constructive feedback that I really needed to learn to put them down for tummy time. And that way it would help them. I found out later it would actually help pass gas for the child that way too. And I think it was just a really big moment for me to learn that the approach that I would have taken originally doesn't always have to be the right one. And that it's good to listen to the other teachers and accept help in departments that I might not be as familiar with.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time you had a challenge with another adult. How did you navigate it?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q8 Attempt 1]
One of the children ended up having scratches and it was very alarming to see when you go to change a day for a lot of scratches everywhere. And it was with a more reactive parent that we did have in the class. And it was very difficult finding a very tactful way to just kind of feel out and ask where these could be coming from. She did immediately become very, and rightfully so, no parent wants to feel like they're being questioned. She became very defensive. And then we did find out later, because she didn't want to really respond, we did find out that she had just gotten a cat and the cat was very active. And it was a learning curve between them to try to figure out how to get the cat and have a small child. But yeah. We ended up talking it out. I ended up scheduling an extra appointment to sit down with them. I brought us both coffee so we could sit down and make sure she knew that this was no ill will. I just, I just wanted to talk and to reassure her she was a good parent and that, you know, it was just, I would want my own child to have someone brought it up if they ended up coming to school with scratches to inquire what was wrong. And so we ended up talking and we had a stronger relationship later on down the road because of it.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about how you physically care for infants or toddlers during routines like feeding, diapering, or comforting.
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q10 Attempt 1]
Okay. So with routines like diapering, I try to always make sure I announce what we're doing and talk them through the process. It's very important, even at a young age, that they always kind of hear these things. So nothing is, they, so you never make them feel like they're just being handled. It's very important that depending on the age, you make sure you support their heads, their bodies. You make sure that you're always interacting with them and talking to them. You're checking on them to see if they seem fussy, if they seem upset, because they can't verbalize anything. If they start crying early on, you have to make sure that you check for things like rashes and that their diaper's fitting correctly, that it's the right size.
